feedback: If a child predicts 'it makes no difference where the pivot is', have them measure both positions: the force-meter reading visibly changes, so pivot and effort position matter.

If a child says the lever 'lifts for free' or 'makes you stronger', ask what their end of the bar had to do — show the effort end moves much further than the load rises, so the smaller force is paid for by the greater distance moved; nothing is free.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A smaller force lifts the load because the pivot is close to the load and the effort is far from it, and the cost is that your end moves a longer way.'
activities.intendedInsight: As the pivot moves closer to the load, so that the effort is applied further from the pivot than the load is, the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops. A smaller force has a greater effect, but the effort end travels a longer distance. You apply a smaller force at the cost of moving further. The lever does not create energy: the bigger force on the load is paid for by your end moving further.
learnerActions: Set up a stiff ruler or rod across a movable pivot (e.g. a pencil or small log), with a fixed mass as the load near one end.
Before testing, predict: as you move the pivot toward the load (and apply the effort further from the pivot), will the effort needed go up or down — and why? Write or say your prediction.
Hook a force meter at the effort end (or push and feel the effort) and read the effort needed to lift the fixed load with the pivot in its first position.
Slide the pivot closer to the load, repeat the measurement, and record how the force-meter reading changes.
Notice and describe what your hand/the effort end has to do: how far it moves compared with how far the load rises.
activities.title: Measure the effort drop on a real lever (predict-then-measure)

feedback: If a child swaps effort and load on a wheelbarrow or tweezers, have them identify what is being lifted (load) versus where they apply force (effort), then find the fixed pivot.
If a child says gears are only in bikes and cars, show an egg-whisk or clock; if they think a pulley only hangs from a ceiling, show a movable pulley that reduces effort.

Reinforce: on a lever like the ruler or seesaw, where the pivot is between the load and the effort and you push at the far end, moving the pivot toward the load reduces the effort needed. This matches what the measurement and workbench showed. Remember that some levers, like tweezers, need more effort instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Grounding the abstraction in familiar objects, and correctly locating effort/load/pivot even in awkward arrangements, consolidates the vocabulary and challenges over-narrow images (gears only in bikes/cars; pulleys only fixed overhead).
learnerActions: On a lever diagram, label the load (object being lifted), the effort (force you apply) and the pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — learn 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same thing.
Sort everyday objects into lever, pulley or gear: seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint, egg-whisk, flagpole pulley.
For each lever example, mark where the effort, load and pivot are — including trickier arrangements like the wheelbarrow and tweezers.

Match each mechanism to what it changes: a lever reduces the effort when the effort is further from the pivot than the load is (e.g. crowbar, bottle opener, wheelbarrow), but some levers, such as tweezers and the elbow, need a larger effort in exchange for a bigger, faster or more precise movement at the load; a pulley changes direction and (with an extra movable wheel) reduces effort; gears change the size and/or direction of the turning force and the speed of turning.
Answer prediction prompts such as: 'Move the pivot toward the load — does the effort go up or down?'
activities.title: Name the parts and classify everyday machines

feedback: If a gear train won't turn, check the cogs mesh; link the small-fast/large-slow behaviour back to what they saw in gear mode.
If adding a movable pulley doesn't seem to help, count the supporting ropes and relate more ropes to lower effort but a greater length of rope to pull.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically assembling mechanisms adds tangibility and an engineering feel, letting children see how real spacing and meshing produce the force/direction/speed changes modelled elsewhere.
learnerActions: Assemble a simple gear train with different-sized cogs and turn the driver; observe which gear turns faster and which turns with more force.
Rig a real pulley with a string and hanging load, then add a movable wheel to build a simple block-and-tackle; feel the effort change and note any change in pull direction.
Describe how the physical assembly (spacing, meshing, number of supporting ropes) affects what the mechanism does.
activities.title: Build-and-test extension: gear trains and a block-and-tackle
